personas.role: Issues the card behind the agentic token, is enabled for Agent Pay at network level, and makes the final authorization decision.
goals: Approve good agent purchases without extra friction
See clearly when an agent was involved
Keep fraud and dispute rates flat as agent traffic grows
pains: No public agent-specific reason codes or liability terms; Mastercard's rules refer to Agent Pay Program Standards that are not public
Agent flags that are not always present, hence the probability score rolling out for US testing (announced 2026-09-30)
Verifiable Intent evidence that is not yet documented inside live authorizations
implements: Passkey authentication for consumer consent where offered
Authorization rules that read the additional information in the message
mustTrust: Mastercard to register and certify agents
The network to detokenize and enforce token limits
The agent platform to capture the consumer intent accurately
questions: Which data element tells me an agent initiated this transaction?
Who carries the loss when an agent buys the wrong thing within its limits?
Can I read a Verifiable Intent chain today, or only later?
firstSteps: Confirm with Mastercard that your BINs are enabled for Agent Pay
Map how agent transactions appear in your authorization and dispute systems
Read the Verifiable Intent security model and its dispute evidence section
metrics: Fraud and dispute rate on agent transactions
Share of agent transactions that carry reliable agent information
personas.story: Priya runs card authorization strategy at a mid-sized European bank. On 2026-06-02 Mastercard said all its European issuers were enabled for Agent Pay at network level, so agent transactions may already reach her systems. She wants to approve them without new friction, but her dispute team asks a hard question: when a cardholder says the agent bought the wrong hotel, which reason code applies? None is public: Mastercard's rules refer participants to Agent Pay Program Standards that are not public. She asks Mastercard which message field marks agent involvement, sets a rule to review those transactions separately for a quarter, and reads the Verifiable Intent dispute evidence section to see what proof she could ask for later.

personas.role: Mastercard itself: registers and certifies agents, keeps the trusted agent lists, is to host a key directory for its agents, issues and detokenizes agentic tokens, and, under the Verifiable Intent spec, validates Verifiable Intent chains before authorization (no public record of this in production yet).
goals: Make every agent transaction recognizable to every party
Keep raw card numbers away from agents
Set the rules other networks and EMVCo converge on
pains: Agents that still drive human checkout forms
Stateful Verifiable Intent constraints that need new network-side state
Competing formats from Visa, Google and others
implements: Agent registration, security review and trusted agent lists
The probability score for AI-initiated transactions, rolling out for US testing (announced 2026-09-30)
mustTrust: Agent developers to keep signing keys safe
Issuers to make sensible decisions with the additional information
questions: How do we revoke an agent across the network?
Where do we hold budget and occurrence state for Verifiable Intent mandates?
How do our tags and directory align with the IETF Web Bot Auth draft?
firstSteps: Publish a resolvable key directory location
Document a revocation path for agents and Agentic Tokens
Fix the duplicate-digest issue in the Verifiable Intent L2 format
metrics: Share of agent transactions verified with Verifiable Intent
personas.story: Marco works on the network side of Agent Pay. His team certifies agents, keeps the trusted lists and issues the tokens, and since 2026-09-30 it has been rolling out, for US testing, a probability score for transactions that look agent-initiated. That score exists because not every agent purchase arrives with a clean flag. His backlog is long: a key directory location that developers can actually resolve, a revocation path for a misbehaving agent, network-side state for Verifiable Intent budgets, and an open issue saying the L2 format lists digests twice. He starts with the directory, because every merchant verification depends on it.

personas.role: Sells online through an acquirer or PSP and wants agent orders without rebuilding checkout.
goals: Accept agent purchases through the existing card form
pains: Bot defenses that block good agents
Not knowing which agents are registered
No clear dispute rules for agent orders
implements: Registration for Agent Pay through the acquirer or PSP
Web Bot Auth verification, usually at the CDN
Normal card acceptance for tokens typed into the form
mustTrust: The CDN to verify signatures correctly
The acquirer to handle agent transactions like other card payments
questions: Do I need any code change for Level 1?
What happens to an untagged bot?
Who pays if an agent order is disputed?
firstSteps: Ask your acquirer or PSP how to register for Agent Pay
Turn on signed-agent verification at your CDN if it offers it
Test a checkout where the token is typed into your card form
personas.story: Ana runs a small cinema chain website on a hosted platform with Cloudflare in front. She keeps seeing bots in her logs and blocks most of them. Her acquirer tells her that Agent Pay agents sign their requests and that her CDN can check those signatures, while the agent types a token into her normal card form, so her PCI scope stays the same. She registers through the acquirer, switches on signed-agent verification at the edge and leaves her checkout untouched. Her open question is disputes: standard chargeback rules apply, and no agent-specific terms are public, because Mastercard's rules refer to Agent Pay Program Standards that are not public.

personas.role: Builds the agent: registers it with Mastercard, captures consent, requests tokens and signs every merchant request.
goals: Let users buy through the agent at any Mastercard merchant
Pass certification once and reuse it
pains: No public SDK, API reference or sandbox for card Agent Pay (Agent Pay for Machines opened Early Access with APIs and a sandbox on 2026-10-20)
Two spellings of the tag and an example directory host that does not resolve
Form filling on pages built for people
implements: RFC 9421 request signing with the Agent Pay tag
mustTrust: Mastercard to keep the agent listed
Merchants and CDNs to verify signatures
questions: Which tag spelling do verifiers accept?
How do I get a token through Stripe instead of directly?
When will Verifiable Intent be required?
firstSteps: Read the Rails for Agentic Commerce and Level 1 guides
Prototype signing with RFC 9421 and test against a CDN
Run the Verifiable Intent Python examples locally
personas.story: Sam leads payments at a startup building a shopping agent. He wants users to say "book two tickets for Friday" and have the agent finish the purchase at any merchant. Agent Pay requires a registered key, a security review and tokens instead of card numbers, which suits him, but the card path has no public SDK or sandbox. He signs requests with RFC 9421 and tests both spellings of the tag. For merchants on Stripe he considers Shared Payment Tokens, which carry Mastercard agentic tokens. He also runs the Verifiable Intent examples, expecting signed intent to become part of certification.

personas.role: Models fraud and disputes for an issuer, acquirer or merchant, and decides how agent transactions are scored and reviewed.
goals: Avoid blanket declines of agent purchases
pains: No public description of the agent information or the probability score fields
Verifiable Intent has no revocation protocol in 0.1
implements: Rules keyed on agent indicators and signature verification results
Review queues for deferred orders that fail intent validation
mustTrust: The network's agent information and score
questions: How reliable is the agent information today?
What does a Verifiable Intent chain prove in a dispute?
Which attacks does the threat model leave open?
firstSteps: List the agent signals you receive today
Read the Verifiable Intent security model
Ask the network for probability score documentation
metrics: Fraud basis points on agent transactions
personas.story: Lena runs fraud strategy for an acquirer. Agent transactions are still a small slice, but her models treat form-filling agents like bots. Mastercard's 2026-09-30 probability score tells her the network itself does not always know when an agent was involved. She reads the Verifiable Intent threat model and likes what it covers, replay, constraint stripping and split-agent attacks, but notes that version 0.1 has no revocation protocol. She sets up a separate review queue for agent orders and asks her network contact what the score looks like in the message.

personas.role: Holds the Mastercard card, authorizes an agent with a passkey and sets its limits.
goals: Keep the real card number private
Get money back if the agent gets it wrong
pains: Unclear rules when an agent buys the wrong item within its limits
Little visibility into which agents are trusted
implements: Merchant, amount and time limits for the agent
mustTrust: The agent platform to follow instructions
The issuer to honor dispute rights
questions: Can the agent see my card number?
How do I stop the agent?
firstSteps: Check that your bank supports Agent Pay
Set tight merchant and amount limits
Review your statement for agent purchases
personas.story: Tom asks his assistant app to book a ski weekend under a set budget. The app asks him to confirm with a passkey and to choose limits: this merchant, this amount, this weekend. It never sees his card number; it gets an agentic token that works only within those limits. If the booking is wrong he can dispute it with his bank like any card purchase, because standard chargeback rights apply. What he cannot find is a simple button to stop one agent everywhere, so he plans to keep limits tight and short.

rows.step: Register agent key and pass certification
Verify signature at edge or backend
